topic: Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience & Language
subject: religious-studies

items.correct: Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
items.misconception: Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
items.random_wrong: Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
items.why: Each Way is a self-standing argument with different structure. Students treat them as a single chain, missing that Aquinas offered multiple independent routes — the failure of one doesn't undermine the others.

items.q: What are James's four characteristics of mystical experience?
items.correct: Ineffability (beyond words), noetic quality (gives knowledge), transience (temporary), and passivity (feeling acted upon by something greater).
items.misconception: Religious experiences are just hallucinations caused by stress.
items.random_wrong: Religious experiences only happen during dreams.
items.why: James was a psychologist describing common features, not assessing truth. Students collapse the question of describing experience into the question of whether God caused it — distinct issues.

items.q: What is the problem of evil?
items.correct: If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
items.misconception: It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
items.random_wrong: It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
items.why: Students treat it as a moral or eschatological question. It is actually a logical challenge to classical theism — and the central problem theodicies try to solve.

items.q: Does Swinburne's principle of credulity prove religious experiences are veridical?
items.correct: No — it creates a defeasible presumption: if it seems to someone that God is present, that is prima facie evidence, which can be overridden by reasons to doubt (drugs, unreliability, conflicting claims).
items.misconception: Swinburne's principle of credulity proves that religious experiences are genuine encounters with God.
items.random_wrong: Swinburne's principle says all experiences must be doubted until verified in a laboratory.
items.why: Credulity shifts the burden of proof; it does not settle the question. Students upgrade 'prima facie evidence' into 'proof', missing the defeaters Swinburne himself lists.

items.q: Did Freud claim to have disproved God's existence by calling religion an illusion?
items.correct: No — for Freud an 'illusion' is a belief produced by wishes; he held this made religion suspect, but acknowledged an illusion is not necessarily false.
items.misconception: Freud scientifically proved that God does not exist and that all religious experiences are fake.
items.random_wrong: Freud believed religious experiences were genuine messages from the unconscious mind of God.
items.why: In The Future of an Illusion, Freud distinguishes illusion (wish-derived) from delusion (false). His critique undermines the rational credentials of belief without strictly disproving it — a nuance examiners reward.
The answer examiners want is: Aquinas. “Anselm” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.
Correct answer: Hume. “Descartes” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: How many of Aristotle's causes are there?
items.why: Exact answer: 4 causes. Estimation gets you near it; only the anchored number survives the exam hall.
